mainTopic: Which things may be said in any language, and which only in לשון הקודש: שמע, תפלה, ברכת המזון, oaths, ביכורים and חליצה.
overview: The amud continues the משנה's two lists: things that may be said in any language, and things that must be said only in לשון הקודש. First the גמרא asks whether the מחלוקת between רבי and רבנן about קריאת שמע shows what each side holds about the rest of the תורה. It answers no, because each side needs its own word only to cancel the other word in the פסוק. Next it explains that תפלה may be said in any language, because it is a request for רחמים. It challenges this from רבי יוחנן's statement that the angels do not understand Aramaic, and answers that his warning applies to a יחיד while the משנה is about a ציבור. When a בת קול is shown to have spoken Aramaic, the גמרא answers that a בת קול is different, or that the voice was גבריאל, who knows every language. Then it gives the sources for ברכת המזון, שבועת העדות and שבועת הפקדון being allowed in any language. Finally it shows why מקרא ביכורים must be in Hebrew, through a chain of two גזירה שוה comparisons, and explains how רבי יהודה and רבנן read the word "ככה" in the פסוק about חליצה.

steps.title: Does רבי hold that the rest of the תורה may be said in any language?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that רבי holds the whole תורה may be said in any language. Otherwise, he would not need a special word ("וְהָיוּ") to require Hebrew for שמע.
steps.simpleTranslation: [Shall we say רבי holds that] the whole תורה may be said in any language? Because if you thought the whole תורה must be said in לשון הקודש, why would the תורה need to write "וְהָיוּ" to teach this about שמע?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing a question it began just before this. It suggests that רבי's reading of "וְהָיוּ" shows he thinks the rest of the תורה may be said in any language.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The logic is: if every part of the תורה already had to be in Hebrew, a special word to make שמע Hebrew-only would be extra. Since רבי needs "וְהָיוּ" for שמע, it looks like the rest of the תורה is not Hebrew-only in his view. The step that follows will test whether this inference really holds.

keyTerms.meaning: The holy tongue, meaning Hebrew.
In any language.
"For if it would enter your mind," a formula used to set up the opposite view and show it doesn't work.
"The Merciful One," a name for ה׳, used when quoting the תורה.
"Why do I need it?" The verse would seem to be extra.

phrases.english: [that] the entire Torah may be said in any language,
for if it would enter your mind
that it must be said in the holy tongue,
"and they shall be," which the Merciful One wrote,
phrases.notes: דברים 6:6. רבי reads it as "the words shall stay as they are," meaning in Hebrew.

phrases.english: why do I need it?

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאִי סָלְקָא דַּעְתָּךְ בִּלְשׁוֹן הַקּוֹדֶשׁ נֶאֶמְרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: This continues the "shall we say" question from just before, about what רבי holds.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does רבי's need for "וְהָיוּ" prove he holds that the rest of the תורה may be said in any language?

steps.title: רבי needs "וְהָיוּ" only because "שְׁמַע" is also written
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof. רבי needs "וְהָיוּ" because otherwise the word "שְׁמַע" would have taught that שמע may be said in any language.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is needed, because "שְׁמַע" is written.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the suggestion in step 1. "וְהָיוּ" is not extra, because it is needed to cancel what we might have learned from the word "שְׁמַע".
steps.deeperAnalysis: Without "וְהָיוּ", someone could read "שְׁמַע" the way רבנן do, as "in any language you understand." So רבי needs "וְהָיוּ" to block that reading, even if the rest of the תורה is Hebrew-only. That means no proof about the rest of the תורה can be drawn from רבי.

keyTerms.meaning: "It is needed." The verse is not extra after all.
"Because it is written."
"Hear." רבנן read it as "in any language you hear and understand."

phrases.english: It is needed,
because "hear" is written.
phrases.notes: דברים 6:4. Without "וְהָיוּ", we might have learned "any language" from this word.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the inference from step 1 by showing that "וְהָיוּ" has a real job.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the whole proof about what רבי holds for the rest of the תורה.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: "וְהָיוּ" is not extra. It is needed to counter the possible "any language" reading of "שְׁמַע".

steps.title: Do רבנן hold that the whole תורה must be said in Hebrew?
steps.stepSummary: Now the גמרא tries the opposite direction. Maybe רבנן hold the whole תורה must be in Hebrew. Otherwise, why would they need "שְׁמַע" to allow any language for שמע?
steps.simpleTranslation: Shall we say רבנן hold that the entire תורה must be said in לשון הקודש? Because if you thought it may be said in any language, why would the תורה need to write "שְׁמַע"?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns the same kind of question onto רבנן. It suggests that their need for "שְׁמַע" shows they think the rest of the תורה must be in Hebrew.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the mirror image of step 1. If the whole תורה could already be said in any language, a special word allowing any language for שמע would be extra. So it seems רבנן think the rest of the תורה is Hebrew-only.

keyTerms.meaning: "Shall we say?" The גמרא is suggesting an idea in order to test it.
"The Rabbis hold." These are the חכמים who say שמע may be said in any language.
"All of it," stressing the entire תורה.

phrases.english: Shall we say the Rabbis hold
that the entire Torah, all of it,
must be said in the holy tongue?
For if it would enter your mind that it may be said in any language,
why do I need "hear," which the Merciful One wrote?

steps.triggerLanguage: לֵימָא קָסָבְרִי רַבָּנַן כׇּל הַתּוֹרָה כּוּלָּהּ בִּלְשׁוֹן קוֹדֶשׁ נֶאֶמְרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the same reasoning as step 1, but now applied to רבנן.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does רבנן's need for "שְׁמַע" prove they hold that the rest of the תורה must be said in Hebrew?

steps.title: רבנן need "שְׁמַע" only because "וְהָיוּ" is also written
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects this proof too. רבנן need "שְׁמַע" because otherwise "וְהָיוּ" would have taught that שמע must be in Hebrew.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is needed, because "וְהָיוּ" is written.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on step 3 the same way it did in step 2. "שְׁמַע" is needed to cancel what we might have learned from "וְהָיוּ".
steps.deeperAnalysis: Without "שְׁמַע", someone could read "וְהָיוּ" the way רבי does and require Hebrew. So רבנן need "שְׁמַע" to allow any language, even if the rest of the תורה may already be said in any language. That means no proof can be drawn from רבנן either.

keyTerms.meaning: The daily reading of שמע, which is the subject of the מחלוקת.
A verse. Both words, "שְׁמַע" and "וְהָיוּ", come from the same section of the תורה.
A disagreement, here between רבי and רבנן.

steps.whatToRemember: Each side needs its own word only to cancel the other word in the פסוק. So the מחלוקת between רבי and רבנן about שמע proves nothing about whether the rest of the תורה may be said in any language.

phrases.english: It is needed,
because "and they shall be" is written.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the inference from step 3, matching the rejection in step 2.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the whole proof about what רבנן hold for the rest of the תורה.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: "שְׁמַע" is not extra. It is needed to counter the possible Hebrew-only reading of "וְהָיוּ".

steps.title: Why prayer may be said in any language
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains the משנה's rule that תפלה may be said in any language: תפלה is a request for רחמים, so a person may pray however he wants.
steps.simpleTranslation: Prayer is a request for mercy, so a person may pray in any way he wants.
steps.whatsHappening: Steps 1-4 dealt with שמע. Now the גמרא moves to the next item in the משנה, תפלה, and gives the reason it may be said in any language.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The reason is about what תפלה is. It is a personal plea for רחמים, not a fixed text read from the תורה. A plea counts in any language the person understands and means.

keyTerms.meaning: Prayer; here, the שמונה עשרה (עמידה)
A request for mercy
Any way that he wants
He prays

phrases.english: Prayer: it is a request for mercy,
so any way that he wants, he may pray.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the discussion of שמע to the next item in the משנה, תפלה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: תפלה may be said in any language because it is a request for רחמים.

steps.title: Challenge: angels ignore requests in Aramaic
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the rule from רב יהודה, who quotes רבי יוחנן: a person should not ask for his needs in Aramaic, because the מלאכי השרת do not understand Aramaic and will not help him.
steps.simpleTranslation: Can prayer really be said in any language? רב יהודה said a person should never ask for his needs in Aramaic. רבי יוחנן said that the angels do not help someone who asks in Aramaic, because they do not understand it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the rule from step 5. It shows a statement saying that at least one language, Aramaic, is a problem for prayer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the angels ignore Aramaic requests, then praying in Aramaic is not a good way to pray. That seems to contradict the משנה's claim that תפלה works in any language.

keyTerms.meaning: His needs
The Aramaic language
The ministering angels
Attend to him, take care of his request
Are familiar with, recognize

steps.confusionAlert: רבי יוחנן is not saying Aramaic prayer is forbidden or invalid. He says the angels will not help bring the request up, because they do not know the language.

phrases.english: And may prayer really be said in any language?
But didn't Rav Yehuda say:
A person should never ask for his needs
in the Aramaic language,
as Rabbi Yochanan said:
Anyone who asks for his needs in Aramaic,
the ministering angels do not attend to him,
because the ministering angels are not
familiar with the Aramaic language!

steps.triggerLanguage: וּתְפִלָּה בְּכׇל לָשׁוֹן? וְהָאָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the rule just explained in step 5.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's rule that תפלה may be said in any language.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי יוחנן says Aramaic requests are not taken up by the angels, so not every language works for תפלה.

steps.title: Answer: individual versus community
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that רבי יוחנן is talking about a יחיד praying alone, while the משנה is talking about תפלה בציבור.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not a contradiction: one statement is about a person praying alone, and the other is about a community praying together.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא settles the contradiction from step 6 by giving each statement its own case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A יחיד needs the angels to help his prayer go up, so a language they do not understand is a problem for him. A ציבור's prayer is accepted even without the angels' help, so any language works. Both statements are true, each in its own situation.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult; there is no contradiction
This one... that one (splitting two sources into two cases)
An individual praying alone
A community, a group praying together

steps.whatToRemember: The משנה's 'any language' applies to תפלה בציבור. A יחיד should avoid asking for his needs in Aramaic.

phrases.english: It is not difficult:
this one is about an individual,
phrases.notes: 'This one' is רבי יוחנן's warning about Aramaic.

phrases.english: that one is about a community.
phrases.notes: 'That one' is the משנה, which allows any language.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא קַשְׁיָא: הָא בְּיָחִיד, הָא בְּצִבּוּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 6.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (אוקימתא): each source applies to a different situation.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה seemed to allow any language for every תפלה, which clashes with רבי יוחנן.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה is about a ציבור; רבי יוחנן's warning is about a יחיד, who needs the angels' help.

steps.title: Challenge: a heavenly voice spoke Aramaic
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבי יוחנן's claim that the angels do not understand Aramaic. A ברייתא tells of two בת קול messages from the קודש הקדשים, heard by יוחנן כהן גדול and שמעון הצדיק, and both were in Aramaic.
steps.simpleTranslation: Do the angels really not understand Aramaic? A ברייתא teaches that יוחנן כהן גדול heard a בת קול from the קודש הקדשים say: 'The young men who went to fight at Antioch have won.' Another time שמעון הצדיק heard a בת קול from the קודש הקדשים say: 'The enemy's plan against the בית המקדש is cancelled, גסקלגס has been killed, and his decrees are cancelled.' People wrote down the time, and it matched exactly. And the voice spoke in Aramaic!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now questions the reason behind רבי יוחנן's statement, that the angels do not know Aramaic. The answer will come next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A בת קול comes from heaven, so if it spoke Aramaic, heavenly beings must know Aramaic. Writing down the time and seeing it matched shows the message was real. That seems to disprove the claim that the מלאכי השרת do not understand Aramaic.

keyTerms.meaning: A heavenly voice
The Holy of Holies, the innermost room of the בית המקדש
They matched, the timing lined up exactly

phrases.aramaic: וְאֵין מַלְאֲכֵי הַשָּׁרֵת מַכִּירִין בִּלְשׁוֹן אֲרַמִּי?
phrases.english: And are the ministering angels really not familiar with Aramaic?
But wasn't it taught in a baraita:

phrases.aramaic: יוֹחָנָן כֹּהֵן גָּדוֹל שָׁמַע בַּת קוֹל
phrases.english: Yochanan the High Priest heard a heavenly voice
from the Holy of Holies that was saying:
The young men have won,
phrases.notes: These words of the voice are in Aramaic, and that is the whole point of the question.

phrases.english: the ones who went to wage war at Antioch.
And there was another incident with Shimon HaTzaddik,
who heard a heavenly voice
from the Holy of Holies that was saying:
The plan is cancelled
that the enemy said he would bring against the Temple,
and Gaskalgas has been killed and his decrees are cancelled.
phrases.notes: Gaskalgas is the Roman emperor Caligula.

phrases.english: And they wrote down that time, and it matched exactly.
And it was speaking in Aramaic!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאֵין מַלְאֲכֵי הַשָּׁרֵת מַכִּירִין בִּלְשׁוֹן אֲרַמִּי? וְהָתַנְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Now that step 7 has limited רבי יוחנן's rule to a יחיד, the גמרא attacks the reason behind that rule, which was first stated in step 6.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוחנן's reason that the מלאכי השרת do not understand Aramaic.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A בת קול from the קודש הקדשים spoke in Aramaic, so heaven clearly knows Aramaic.

steps.title: A Divine Voice is different
steps.stepSummary: First answer: a בת קול is meant to be heard by people, so it may speak Aramaic even though angels do not understand it.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you want, you can say: a בת קול is different, because its whole purpose is to let people hear a message.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from step 8. The Aramaic בת קול messages do not prove that angels understand Aramaic.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן said angels do not understand Aramaic, but the בת קול spoke in Aramaic. The answer is that a בת קול is made to talk to people. So it speaks in the language the people understand, and this says nothing about what the angels understand.

keyTerms.meaning: If you wish, say. This introduces one possible answer, and often a second one follows.
A heavenly voice
Is different
To let someone hear, to tell a message

phrases.english: If you wish, say:
a Divine Voice is different,
since it is made to let people hear a message.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי בָּעֵית אֵימָא: בַּת קוֹל שָׁאנֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 8
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinction: a בת קול is a special case, so it does not show what angels understand
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Aramaic from the קודש הקדשים shows that heavenly beings understand Aramaic
steps.terutzMaskana: A בת קול speaks so that people will hear it, so its language says nothing about the angels

steps.title: It was גבריאל, who knows seventy languages
steps.stepSummary: Second answer: the voice was the angel גבריאל, who knows all seventy languages, unlike the other angels.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or, if you want, say that it was גבריאל. As the Master said: גבריאל came and taught him seventy languages.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a different answer to the same challenge. The Aramaic voice came from גבריאל, who is an exception among the angels.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן's rule is about angels in general. גבריאל is special because he knows every language, as we see from the teaching that he taught seventy languages. So an Aramaic message from him does not contradict רבי יוחנן.

keyTerms.meaning: The angel גבריאל
Seventy languages, meaning all the languages of the world

steps.whatToRemember: רבי יוחנן's rule still stands. Either a בת קול is different, or the voice was גבריאל, who knows every language.

phrases.english: And if you wish, say:
it was Gabriel.
As the Master said:
Gabriel came and taught him seventy languages.
phrases.notes: "Him" is יוסף. If גבריאל could teach every language, he must know them all himself.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second, different answer to the challenge of step 8
steps.terutzResolutionType: Exception: one angel is different from the rest
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The voice shows that angels understand Aramaic
steps.terutzMaskana: Only גבריאל knows every language. The other angels still do not understand Aramaic.

steps.title: Source that ברכת המזון may be said in any language
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא returns to the משנה's list and learns from "וברכת" that ברכת המזון may be said in any language.
steps.simpleTranslation: ברכת המזון may be said in any language, as it is written: "And you shall eat and be satisfied and bless ה׳ your God." This means: in any language in which you bless.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the list in the משנה and gives the source for the next item, ברכת המזון.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says simply "and you shall bless" and names no language. So the גמרא reads it as: bless in whatever language you bless in.

keyTerms.meaning: The blessing said after eating, Grace after Meals
As it is written
In any language

phrases.english: Grace after Meals:
as it is written:
"And you shall eat and be satisfied,
and bless the Lord your God"
in any language in which you bless.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the discussion of תפלה and moves to the next item in the משנה
steps.mimraCoreRuling: ברכת המזון may be said in any language, because the פסוק does not name a language.

steps.title: Source that שבועת העדות may be said in any language
steps.stepSummary: From "ושמעה קול אלה" the גמרא learns that שבועת העדות works in any language the person hears, meaning understands.
steps.simpleTranslation: שבועת העדות may be said in any language, as it is written: "And if a person sins, and hears the voice of an oath." This means: in any language that the person hears.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the source for the next item in the משנה, שבועת העדות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק stresses that the person "hears" the oath. Hearing here means understanding. So any language the witness understands is good enough.

keyTerms.meaning: The oath of testimony, when witnesses swear they know nothing about a case
An oath, a curse
Hears, and here also understands

phrases.english: An oath of testimony:
as it is written:
"And if a person sins,
and hears the voice of an oath"
in any language that she hears.
phrases.notes: "She" is the "נפש", the person. "Hears" means understands.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues going through the משנה's list
steps.mimraCoreRuling: שבועת העדות works in any language the person understands.

steps.title: שבועת הפקדון is learned from שבועת העדות
steps.stepSummary: Using a גזירה שוה on the word "תחטא", the גמרא learns that שבועת הפקדון, like שבועת העדות, may be said in any language.
steps.simpleTranslation: An oath about a deposit: this is learned from the word "sins" here and the word "sins" in the oath of testimony.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the source for שבועת הפקדון. Here there is no direct פסוק, so it learns it from שבועת העדות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both sections in the תורה use the word "תחטא" (sins). This shared word links them in a גזירה שוה. So the rule of שבועת העדות, that it works in any language, applies to שבועת הפקדון too.

keyTerms.meaning: An oath that a person denies holding someone else's deposit or money
It comes from, it is learned from
Learning one law from another because the same word appears in both

steps.whatToRemember: Each item in the משנה has its own source. ברכת המזון comes from "וברכת", שבועת העדות from "ושמעה", and שבועת הפקדון from a גזירה שוה with שבועת העדות.

phrases.english: An oath on a deposit:
is learned from "sins" and "sins"
phrases.notes: This is a גזירה שוה: the same word shows up in ויקרא 5:21 (about a deposit) and ויקרא 5:1 (about testimony).

phrases.english: from the oath of testimony.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on step 12 by borrowing its rule through a גזירה שוה
steps.mimraCoreRuling: שבועת הפקדון may be said in any language, just like שבועת העדות.

steps.title: First fruits recitation must be in the holy tongue
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's list of things said only in לשון הקודש, and its proof for מקרא ביכורים: the word "וענית" is learned from the same kind of word ("וענו") used about the לוים.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says: these must be said in Hebrew, including מקרא ביכורים and חליצה. How do we know מקרא ביכורים must be in Hebrew? The תורה says "you shall speak up and say," and later it says "the לוים shall speak up and say." Just as the לוים spoke in Hebrew, so too מקרא ביכורים is in Hebrew.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now moves to the second list in the משנה, the things that must be said only in לשון הקודש, and quotes how the משנה proves this for מקרא ביכורים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word "וענית" (speak up) appears by ביכורים, and "וענו" appears by the לוים at the blessings and curses. Since the לוים spoke in לשון הקודש, the same rule carries over to ביכורים. This proof only works if we already know the לוים spoke in Hebrew, and that is exactly what the next step asks.

keyTerms.meaning: The holy tongue, meaning Hebrew
The passage a person reads aloud when bringing first fruits to the בית המקדש
The ceremony that frees a widow from יבום when her brother-in-law refuses to marry her
Speaking up or calling out, from the words "וענית" and "וענו"

phrases.english: And these are said in the holy tongue:
the first fruits recitation, and חליצה, etc., until
the first fruits recitation, how so?
"And you shall speak up and say before ה׳ your God"
and further on it says

phrases.aramaic: ״וְעָנוּ הַלְוִיִּם וְאָמְרוּ אֶל כׇּל אִישׁ יִשְׂרָאֵל״,
phrases.english: "And the Levites shall speak up and say to every man of Israel"
phrases.notes: דברים 27:14, the blessings and curses at הר גריזים and הר עיבל.

phrases.english: just as the "speaking up" mentioned there is in the holy tongue
so too here, it is in the holy tongue.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the list of things that may be said in any language to the list of things that must be said in Hebrew.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: מקרא ביכורים must be said in לשון הקודש, learned from the shared word "עניה" ("וענית" / "וענו") with the לוים.

steps.title: How do we know the Levites spoke Hebrew?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the source that the לוים themselves spoke in לשון הקודש.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the לוים themselves, how do we know they spoke in Hebrew?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a follow-up question about the proof it just quoted. It wants to know how we know the לוים spoke Hebrew.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof for ביכורים rests on the לוים speaking in Hebrew. If that is not proven, the comparison has nothing to stand on, so the גמרא asks for its source.

keyTerms.meaning: Themselves
How do we know? A request for a source

phrases.english: And the Levites themselves, how do we know?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the base of the comparison used in step 14.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source that the לוים spoke in לשון הקודש.

steps.title: Learned from משה through the word "voice"
steps.stepSummary: A גזירה שוה of "קול" connects the לוים to משה at מתן תורה, where the speech was in לשון הקודש.
steps.simpleTranslation: We learn it from the word "voice" that appears both here and by משה. Here it says "a loud voice," and there it says "משה spoke, and God answered him with a voice." Just as there it was in Hebrew, so too here it was in Hebrew.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by linking the word "קול" by the לוים to the word "קול" at מתן תורה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: At מתן תורה, God spoke to משה in לשון הקודש. Since the לוים also spoke with a "קול", their words must have been in לשון הקודש too. This completes the chain: מתן תורה leads to the לוים, and the לוים lead to ביכורים.

keyTerms.meaning: It comes from, meaning it is learned from
A loud voice
It is written here... and it is written there. The standard wording of a גזירה שוה

steps.whatToRemember: There is a chain of two comparisons: ביכורים is learned from the לוים through "וענית" / "וענו", and the לוים are learned from מתן תורה through "קול".

phrases.english: It is learned from "voice" and "voice" from Moshe.
It is written here: "a loud voice"
phrases.notes: דברים 27:14, the same פסוק about the לוים.

phrases.english: and it is written there:
"Moshe spoke, and God answered him with a voice"
just as there it was in the holy tongue,
so too here it was in the holy tongue.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 15.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A גזירה שוה of "קול" from מתן תורה, which was in לשון הקודש.

steps.title: What do the Rabbis learn from the word "thus"?
steps.stepSummary: On the משנה's case of חליצה, where רבי יהודה learns Hebrew from "ככה", the גמרא asks what רבנן do with that word.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says: "חליצה, how so?" And the רבנן, what do they do with this word "ככה"?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the משנה's line about חליצה and asks what the רבנן learn from the word "ככה".
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה, רבי יהודה learns from "ככה" (thus) that the words at חליצה must be said in Hebrew. The רבנן learn that rule some other way, so the word "ככה" seems unused by them. The גמרא asks what lesson they take from it.

keyTerms.meaning: Thus, in this way
What do they do with it? Meaning, what do they learn from this word?
The Sages, the majority opinion

steps.confusionAlert: Both רבנן and רבי יהודה agree that חליצה is in Hebrew. They only disagree about which word in the פסוק teaches it.

phrases.english: חליצה, how so? etc.
phrases.notes: This quotes the משנה, where רבי יהודה learns Hebrew from "ככה" in דברים 25:9.

phrases.english: And the Rabbis, this word "thus"
what do they do with it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to the next item in the משנה's list, חליצה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What lesson the רבנן learn from the word "ככה".

steps.title: Only the actions of חליצה are essential
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן use "ככה" to teach that only the action parts of חליצה hold back its validity.
steps.simpleTranslation: They need it to teach that anything that is an action holds back the חליצה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers: the רבנן use "ככה" ("thus shall be done") to teach that the actions of חליצה are essential.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says "ככה יעשה", "thus shall be done", which points to doing. So the actions, such as taking off the shoe, are essential. A missing action makes the חליצה invalid, but missing words do not.

keyTerms.meaning: They need it, meaning they use it for a different lesson
Holds back, meaning it is essential and its absence makes the act invalid
An action

phrases.english: They need it
for this: a thing that is an action is essential.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִיבְּעֵי לְהוּ, לְדָבָר שֶׁהוּא מַעֲשֶׂה מְעַכֵּב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 17.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The רבנן learn from "ככה" that only the actions of חליצה are essential.

steps.title: רבי יהודה learns both lessons from the longer word
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה gets both lessons because the Torah wrote the longer "ככה" instead of the shorter "כה".
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יהודה learns it from the fact that the תורה wrote "ככה" instead of "כה".
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains how רבי יהודה can learn both the rule about actions and the rule about Hebrew from the same word.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is a hidden question here: if "ככה" teaches that the actions are essential, how can רבי יהודה also use it for Hebrew? The answer is that the תורה could have written the short form "כה". The extra letters in "ככה" give room for a second lesson.

keyTerms.meaning: Thus, the shorter form of the word

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yehuda learns it from "thus" (כה) being written as "thus" (ככה).
phrases.notes: The Torah used the longer word, so it teaches two things: the actions are essential, and the words must be in Hebrew.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the implied question of how רבי יהודה gets both lessons.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The extra letters of "ככה" compared with "כה" allow two separate lessons.

steps.title: The Rabbis learn nothing from כה versus ככה
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן do not learn anything from the difference between "כה" and "ככה", so they use the word for only one lesson.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the רבנן do not learn anything from "כה" versus "ככה".
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא closes the topic by explaining why the רבנן do not agree with רבי יהודה's double reading.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For the רבנן, "ככה" and "כה" mean the same thing, so the longer form adds nothing. That leaves the word with only one lesson, that the actions are essential, and they must find the Hebrew rule elsewhere.

keyTerms.meaning: It does not mean anything to them, meaning they do not learn from it

steps.whatToRemember: Both sides agree that the actions of חליצה are essential and that its words are in Hebrew. The only disagreement is whether the longer "ככה" can teach two lessons.

phrases.english: And the Rabbis do not learn anything from "כה" versus "ככה".

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the רבנן's side to balance רבי יהודה's reading in step 19.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The disagreement comes down to whether the longer form "ככה" adds a second lesson. רבי יהודה says it does, and the רבנן say it does not.
